title: Sub-meter tree height mapping of California using aerial images and LiDAR-informed U-Net model
relevance: Trains a U-Net to predict canopy height directly from aerial RGB/NIR using lidar only as training supervision, then applies it wall-to-wall where no lidar exists. This is the single most useful design for us: it converts our 2016 CHM at ~60% coverage from a spatial-and-temporal constraint into a training signal, letting us synthesize a per-year CHM for all 18 acquisitions instead of applying one 2016 snapshot across 2000-2024. It also makes height an auxiliary prediction target rather than an input channel, which is the only version of CHM fusion that survives our vintage mismatch.

authors: Allred, B.W., McCord, S.E. & Morford, S.L.
title: Canopy height model and NAIP imagery pairs across CONUS
relevance: Builds a CONUS-wide paired CHM/NAIP dataset and documents exactly the pairing problems we face: temporal offset between lidar and imagery acquisition, and horizontal misalignment between lidar-derived polygons and NAIP that is worst in heterogeneous terrain. Gives us published tolerances and a screening procedure for deciding which of our 18 acquisitions the 2016 CHM can legitimately be paired with, and where co-registration error will masquerade as height-dependent recall loss. Also a ready-made pretraining corpus if we adopt the Wagner et al. lidar-informed approach.

title: Tree height mapping and crown delineation using LiDAR, large format aerial photographs, and unmanned aerial vehicle photogrammetry in subtropical urban forest
relevance: Urban-forest comparison of lidar-derived versus photogrammetric canopy height for crown delineation, including how height accuracy degrades for short and understory crowns in a built environment. Closest analogue to Edmonds in setting, and it quantifies what a photogrammetric CHM from large-format aerial photography can substitute for lidar - directly relevant to whether our 2000s-era imagery can yield its own height surface. Useful check on whether our 2016 CHM's height bands are reliable at the 5-15 m range where our recall deficit lives.

authors: Zhang, H., Yang, C. & Fan, X.
title: MTCDNet: Multimodal feature fusion-based tree crown detection network using UAV-acquired optical imagery and LiDAR data
relevance: Ablates how CHM should enter the network - as a stacked band versus a separately encoded modality with learned fusion weights - and reports the multiband+CHM combination best (F1 0.8719, IoU 0.7807). Gives us the architecture comparison to cite if we add height as an input channel for the years where the CHM is temporally plausible. The learned-weight fusion is the more defensible option for us because it can downweight the CHM where it is stale or absent, rather than treating a 2016 height as equally valid in 2003 and 2024.

authors: Sierra, S., Ramo, R., Padilla, M. & Cobo, A.
title: Assessing the impact of LiDAR density and input features on forest canopy height estimation through XGBoost, CNN, and CNN + Transformer approaches
relevance: Quantifies how canopy-height estimation degrades as lidar reference density drops and which input features compensate, with CNN+Transformer best under high density (MAE 3.37, R2 0.66) and the ranking changing as density falls. Lets us reason about our ~60% city coverage as a density/sample-size problem with a known accuracy cost rather than an unknown one, and indicates which model class to use given how sparse our supervision actually is. Also a caution on finding 1: an MAE of ~3 m on the height axis would materially blur our 5 m-wide recall bands.
